name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
title: Plagiarism and AI Detection
answer: AI detection tools are unreliable and often misclassify writing by non native English speakers as AI generated, so a detection flag should never by itself lead to a penalty. Instead, a flag should start a conversation with the student about their writing process, using evidence such as draft history to confirm authorship. This matters because accusing a student on the basis of a detection score can cause lasting harm, especially to English learners and students who write in unusual ways.

sections.body: Plagiarism and AI detection concerns the worry many teachers have that students will use AI to complete their work, and the detection tools that claim to identify AI generated text. The problem is that these tools make serious errors, so their output cannot be treated as proof of cheating. The idea is to treat a detection result only as a prompt for discussion rather than as a verdict. This shifts the focus from catching students to understanding how a piece of writing was actually produced. It solves the risk of punishing students unfairly while still taking academic integrity seriously.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a detection flag from a tool such as Turnitin should trigger a conversation with the student about how they wrote the piece. The teacher can look at Google Docs version history to see how the writing developed over time, and a student who can explain their ideas and show their drafts is almost certainly the author. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea, so the same approach applies across year groups. The emphasis is on process evidence, such as drafts and the student's own explanation, rather than on the score itself. This keeps the response proportionate and focused on learning.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research findings. It states that research has found detectors frequently misclassify writing by non native English speakers as generated by AI (Liang et al., 2023). It also notes that custom detectors built for one large assessment performed well, but those are not the tools schools use (Jiang et al., 2024). These findings are the basis for treating detection results with caution.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A flag alone should never lead to a penalty. Accusing a student of cheating based on a detection score can do lasting harm, especially to English learners and students who write in unusual ways. Detection results should only ever start a conversation, and the decision about what happened stays with the teacher who talks with the student and reviews the process evidence. The book points to building academic integrity through process rather than detection, as described in Chapter 6, because that approach protects both integrity and fairness.
